Title: The Case for U.S. Isolationism: Sovereignty, Security, and Savings Through Non-Engagement

Introduction
The United States, as a global superpower, has long sustained a policy of international interventionism, underpinning its foreign policy on alliances, military bases, and political entanglements across the world. Yet, the mounting costs of these engagements—economic, human, and geopolitical—demand a reconsideration of America’s role in global affairs. This essay advocates for a policy of total isolationism, urging the complete withdrawal from international alliances, closure of overseas military bases, and full disengagement from foreign political and military involvement. Such a shift would enhance national security, redirect economic resources to domestic needs, preserve sovereignty, and align with the Founding Fathers’ vision of a nation untethered to foreign intrigue.

1. Economic Rationality: Ending the Drain of Overseas Entanglement

Maintaining the largest military presence in history—over 800 bases in nearly 80 countries—costs the U.S. tens of billions annually. The Department of Defense’s global footprint drains resources that could better serve domestic priorities: crumbling infrastructure, inadequate healthcare, and economic inequality. Closing overseas bases alone could free up $50–$100 billion yearly, unburdening taxpayers and fostering sustainable growth at home.

Moreover, endless wars in Afghanistan, Iraq, and elsewhere have cost over $6 trillion since 2001, according to the Costs of War Project. These funds could fund universal childcare, student loan forgiveness, or climate mitigation. Isolationism dismantles this costly tradition, prioritizing national interests over foreign adventures.

2. National Security Through Non-Intervention

Contrary to the belief that global military presence deters threats, U.S. interventions since 9/11 have multiplied enemies and destabilized regions. The endless cycle of radicalization, drone warfare, and blowback—highlighted by attacks like 9/11 itself—suggests that foreign entanglements breed resentment and incentivize violence against America.

A non-interventionist policy would eliminate strategic vulnerabilities. As historian Andrew Bacevich argues, U.S. military bases function as “bull’s-eyes,” inviting targeted retaliation. Removing this foothold reduces incentives for adversaries to strike, while bolstering homeland defense ensures security through distance, not overreach.

3. Sovereignty and Independence: A Return to Founding Principles

The U.S. Constitution values self-governance, yet international alliances often force America into conflicts that dilute autonomy. NATO, for instance, legally obligates members to defend one another, even against wars distant from U.S. interests—such as a hypothetical Baltic defense pledge. Withdrawal from such commitments empowers Congress to focus on domestic legislation, reducing presidential executive overreach in foreign matters.

Early Americans championed isolationism as a means of preserving sovereignty. George Washington’s Farewell Address cautioned against “entangling alliances,” while Thomas Jefferson’s insistence on “peaceful commerce” with all nations, free of political ties, reflects that ethos. Reclaiming this vision would shield America from foreign political currents and enable self-determination.

4. Ethical Responsibility: Letting Other Nations Resolve Their Conflicts

Militarily "fixing" foreign crises often worsens them. Interventions in Somalia, Syria, and Libya have led to prolonged chaos, displacement, and civilian casualties. The moral imperative is to allow nations to confront their own struggles, minimizing U.S. complicity in unintended carnage.

Isolationism doesn’t equate to indifference; it rejects the delusion that America can—or should—engineer global stability. As scholar Ivan Eland notes, a policy of restraint respects national sovereignty abroad and avoids ethical quandaries of propping up authoritarian regimes (e.g., Saudi Arabia) or arming rival factions in endless proxy wars.

5. Environmental Stewardship: Reducing Global Militarism

Overseas bases and fleets contribute disproportionately to ecological damage. The Department of Defense is the world’s largest institutional emitter of greenhouse gases, generating ecological harm through deforestation, toxic waste, and fossil fuel consumption. Closing bases and downsizing forces would slash emissions, honoring global climate commitments without binding treaties.

Counterargument: "Abandonment Without Consequences?"

Critics argue that isolationism would embolden adversaries like China or Iran, inviting aggression. Yet, U.S. power lies in its economy and technology, not perpetual military occupation. A strategy of “offshore balancing”—dissuading rivals through naval power and alliances closer to their borders—could suffice without global garrisons. Moreover, inward focus ensures diplomatic credibility at home, strengthening U.S. soft power through better domestic example.

Conclusion

Total U.S. isolationism offers a path back to fiscal prudence, peace, and self-determination. Disentangling from alliances, bases, and foreign wars would prioritize economic rejuvenation, security through non-embarrassment, and a return to principles enshrined by America’s founders. As global challenges evolve, the U.S. must ask: Is perpetual intervention the best defense of its values, or a distraction from rebuilding what we have at home? The answer lies in embracing true independence—one free from foreign entanglements.

Final Appeal: The time has come to redefine greatness, not by dominating distant shores but by serving the American people. Isolationism is not retreat; it is reclamation—a chance to safeguard freedom, opportunity, and the Republic itself.

The Case for U.S. Isolationism: Reasons and Supposed Benefits

Isolationism, defined as avoiding global alliances, military interventions, and international organizations, has been periodically advocated as a way for the U.S. to focus entirely on its domestic affairs. Proponents argue that such a policy could enhance national well-being by redirecting resources and attention inward. Below are the key reasons and potential benefits cited by isolationist advocates:

Reasons for Adoption

  1. Reduced Military Spending
    The U.S. defense budget is the largest in the world. Isolationists argue that withdrawing from foreign military engagements could drastically reduce spending, which could instead fund domestic priorities like healthcare, education, infrastructure, or climate initiatives.

  2. Preventing Unnecessary Wars
    By avoiding foreign entanglements, the U.S. would theoretically minimize exposure to conflicts (e.g., Middle East wars, NATO disputes) that do not directly threaten its sovereignty. This would reduce casualties, alleviate public debt tied to war costs, and prevent domestic political polarization caused by divisive military actions.

  3. Sovereignty and Autonomy
    Isolationists claim that participation in international organizations (e.g., the UN, WTO) or treaties (e.g., climate accords) undermines U.S. sovereignty. Exiting these commitments would allow the country to prioritize its own laws, policies, and cultural values without foreign influence.

  4. Economic Protectionism
    Ending trade agreements (e.g., NAFTA, USMCA) and imposing strict tariffs could shield domestic industries from foreign competition. Proponents argue this could boost local manufacturing, jobs, and economic self-reliance, though critics caution this might lead to inflation and trade wars.

  5. Avoiding Geopolitical Risks
    Intervening abroad can create adversaries (e.g., angering nations through sanctions or military actions). Proponents argue that non-intervention reduces the likelihood of retaliation, such as terrorism or cyberattacks driven by foreign resentment.

  6. Moral and Ethical Focus
    Redirecting attention to domestic challenges (e.g., systemic inequality, racial justice, healthcare gaps) could address issues the U.S. often overlooks while critiquing other nations. Isolationism, in this view, would align actions with values like "minding your own business."

  7. Cultural Preservation
    Reduced global engagement might slow the flow of cultural influences (e.g., media, immigration) that some see as diluting perceived U.S. cultural identity. This aligns with arguments for focusing on internal social cohesion.

Supposed Benefits of Isolationism

  1. Economic Redistribution
    Cutting military and foreign aid budgets could free trillions for domestic programs. For example, infrastructure, universal healthcare, and green energy initiatives might be prioritized instead of overseas military bases or interventions.

  2. Improved National Unity
    By avoiding divisive foreign wars and global politics, the government could foster consensus around shared domestic goals (e.g., economic growth, social safety nets) rather than being consumed by international crises or partisan disputes.

  3. Sovereignty and Policy Control
    A non-interventionist stance would allow the U.S. to operate free from international obligations (e.g., human rights scrutiny, climate targets) or economic sanctions from global bodies, maximizing domestic policy independence.

  4. Reduction in Casualties and Trauma
    Fewer military deployments would mean fewer combat deaths and fewer veterans dealing with PTSD or injuries, sparing families and taxpayers the human and financial costs of overseas conflicts.

  5. Lower National Debt
    Reduced international commitments might curb deficit spending, potentially lowering the national debt by decreasing expenditures on foreign aid, arms sales, and peacekeeping missions.

  6. Environmental Focus
    A domestic focus on sustainability—without competing with global climate accords—could accelerate renewable energy adoption and pollution regulation tailored to U.S. needs, rather than adhering to international frameworks viewed as burdensome.

  7. Reduced Terrorism Risks
    Proponents argue that non-intervention would eliminate U.S. foreign policies that inspire anti-American sentiment, thereby reducing motives for terrorism or attacks on U.S. soil.

  8. Simplified Diplomacy
    Abandoning complex geopolitical alliances (e.g., NATO, alliances with Middle Eastern autocracies) would remove diplomatic burdens and reduce the risk of being drawn into crises like civil wars or territorial disputes.

Counterpoints Acknowledged but Framed Within the Isolationist Perspective

While critics argue that isolationism could lead to trade disadvantages, diminished global influence, and worsened international conditions (e.g., humanitarian crises, proliferation of weapons), isolationists counter that:

  • Global Challenges Are Manageable: Problems like pandemics or climate change can be addressed domestically rather than through international frameworks.
  • Self-Sufficiency is Strength: Building a resilient, localized economy might insulate the U.S. from global market fluctuations.
  • Peace Through Neutrality: Non-intervention could reduce global tensions, fostering a world where other nations resolve their own conflicts without U.S. involvement.

Conclusion

Proponents of complete U.S. isolationism contend that disengaging from foreign affairs would redirect resources and energy toward resolving domestic issues, preserving sovereignty, and enhancing national stability. While critics highlight risks like economic stagnation or reduced global leadership, the isolationist argument emphasizes prioritizing American needs and reducing the costs—human, financial, and political—of maintaining a global hegemony. Ultimately, the appeal lies in the belief that a country focused on itself can achieve greater internal harmony and resilience.

Those in favor envision a nation focused inward, unburdened by the financial and human costs of global hegemony, while those opposed argue that such a withdrawal would invite chaos abroad and insecurity at home. The Case for Total American Isolationism: Restoring Sovereignty, Security, and Sanity

The United States of America stands at a crossroads. After more than a century of entangling alliances, endless wars, and bloated global commitments, the time has come to embrace a radical yet necessary course correction: total isolationism. This means the complete withdrawal from all international military and political alliances, the closure of every overseas base, and the full disengagement from foreign conflicts, whether overt or covert. Far from a retreat into irrelevance or weakness, this policy represents the restoration of American sovereignty, the salvation of our economy, the preservation of our military, and the protection of our democratic values. Total isolationism is not cowardice — it is clarity. It is not surrender — it is strength redefined.

I. The Moral Imperative: Endless War is a Betrayal of American Values

Since World War II, the U.S. has waged war nearly continuously — Korea, Vietnam, Grenada, Panama, the Gulf, Somalia, Bosnia, Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, Syria, Yemen… and countless drone strikes and coups in between. These interventions, often justified as promoting “freedom” or “stability,” have resulted in millions of deaths, trillions of dollars wasted, the destabilization of entire regions, and the radicalization of new enemies.

Is this the mission of the United States? Was America founded to be the world’s policeman — or its beacon? The Founding Fathers warned explicitly against “foreign entanglements.” George Washington’s Farewell Address is not dusty relic — it is prophetic wisdom: “The nation which indulges towards another an habitual hatred or an habitual fondness is in some degree a slave.” Jefferson echoed this. Adams declared America “goes not abroad in search of monsters to destroy.” Their vision was of a republic that inspires by example — not by force.

Total isolationism restores American moral authority by ending the hypocrisy of claiming to champion peace while fueling global violence. It recognizes that true virtue lies not in bombing villages to “save” them, but in perfecting our own house. Only then can we genuinely lead — not by coercion, but by inspiration.

II. The Economic Argument: Stop Bleeding Trillions Overseas

The cost of global military hegemony is catastrophic. The U.S. spends more on its military than the next 10 nations combined — often exceeding $800 billion annually. Add in hidden costs — veteran care, interest on war debt, reconstruction boondoggles — and the real tab soars past $6 trillion since 9/11 alone.

Where does this money go? Into the pockets of defense contractors, into the sand of foreign deserts, into the coffers of corrupt regimes. Meanwhile, American infrastructure crumbles. Public education is underfunded. Healthcare remains unaffordable. Homelessness and poverty grow unchecked. The national debt spirals beyond $34 trillion.

Closing 750+ overseas bases and withdrawing from NATO, CENTCOM, AFRICOM, and every other global command would save hundreds of billions annually. Redirecting even a fraction of that spending toward domestic priorities — green energy, universal broadband, vocational training, affordable housing — would transform lives and revive the American Dream. Isolationism is fundamentally an economic stimulus plan for working Americans.

III. The Strategic Reality: Global Policing Makes Us Less Safe

Proponents of intervention claim it “keeps us safe.” The opposite is true. Every drone strike, every regime change, every military occupation breeds resentment, radicalization, and retaliation. The 9/11 Commission concluded that “the abuse of U.S. power” was a primary motivator for the attacks. Blowback is not theory — it is history.

Moreover, the U.S. military is spread dangerously thin. Attempting to dominate every global hotspot means we lack the capacity to defend our own homeland or respond to true existential threats. Taiwan? Ukraine? The Persian Gulf? Why are American sons and daughters dying for interests that do not directly threaten our soil?

Total isolationism allows us to concentrate military power where it belongs: defending American territory, borders, and citizens. Our nuclear deterrent remains intact. Our geographic advantages — two oceans, friendly neighbors — are unchallenged. Let Europe defend Europe. Let Asia sort Asia. Let the Middle East solve its own conflicts. America’s true strategic interest lies in robust homeland defense — not imperial overstretch.

IV. The Constitutional and Democratic Imperative

The U.S. Constitution grants Congress — not the President, not NATO, not the Pentagon — the sole power to declare war. Yet for 80 years, presidents have waged war unilaterally, citing “alliances” or “executive authority.” Congress abdicates. The people are not consulted. This is not democracy — it is oligarchy draped in flags.

Total isolationism restores constitutional order. Without entangling alliances, presidents cannot drag us into wars under the fig leaf of “collective defense.” Closing overseas bases removes the temptation — and logistical capacity — for rapid, unauthorized deployment. Foreign policy would again require Congressional debate, public scrutiny, and democratic consent. Let the people decide — not generals, not lobbyists, not think tank “experts” in Washington salons.

V. The Path to Global Peace — Through Example, Not Empire

Critics will shriek that isolationism invites chaos. But who caused more chaos: the America that stayed home, or the America that invaded, overthrew, and occupied? The world does not need an American empire — it needs an America that thrives in peace, demonstrating that prosperity, liberty, and innovation flourish when a nation focuses on its own people.

Imagine: A United States that invests in AI, quantum computing, and green infrastructure rather than F-35s parked in Qatar. A United States whose diplomats promote trade and cultural exchange — not covert ops and “regime change.” A United States that becomes a sanctuary of stability — not a source of global volatility.

Other nations will adapt. Europe will finally fund its own defense. Japan and South Korea will develop deterrents commensurate with their wealth. Regional powers will assume regional responsibilities. And the American people? We will rediscover civic pride, economic dynamism, and moral purpose — not as rulers of the world, but as masters of our own destiny.

Conclusion: The Courage to Say “Enough”

Total isolationism is not escapism — it is realism. It is not surrender — it is strategic reorientation. It is not weakness — it is the ultimate assertion of strength: the strength to choose peace, to invest in our people, to defend our Constitution, and to reclaim our moral soul.

The age of American empire is bankrupt — morally, financially, strategically. It is time to come home. Close the bases. End the alliances. Withdraw the troops. Redirect the treasure. Let the world manage its own affairs — and let America, at long last, become again what it was meant to be: a city upon a hill, shining not by the light of burning villages, but by the brilliance of its own example.

The greatest act of patriotism is not dying for your country — it is insisting your country stop dying for others.

Let us choose isolationism — not out of fear, but out of wisdom.

Let us choose America — first, last, and always.

The Imperative of Isolation: Why America Must Return Home

For over a century, the United States has acted as the world's preeminent superpower, entangled in a complex web of alliances, military deployments, and interventions spanning the globe. The most compelling argument for isolationism lies in the staggering financial burden borne by the American taxpayer. Maintaining over 750 military bases in more than 80 countries costs taxpayers hundreds of billions annually – funds desperately needed at home. Imagine redirecting these resources towards crumbling infrastructure, an education system struggling to compete globally, a healthcare system in crisis, and the burgeoning national debt. This "empire of bases" consumes vast sums that could revitalize American communities, foster innovation, and ensure domestic prosperity. Isolationism offers the only viable path to claw back these squandered billions and invest them where they belong: within the United States.

Furthermore, entanglement in global affairs demonstrably increases American vulnerability to conflict rather than insulating it. History shows that alliances and forward deployments create obligations and entanglements that drag the US into wars it has no vital national interest in fighting. World War I, a conflict born of tangled European alliances, drew in a reluctant America. More recently, the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, fueled by interventionist ideologies and flawed intelligence, resulted in trillions spent, thousands of American lives lost, and regions left more unstable than before. By abandoning alliances and bases, the US severs these automatic triggers. It removes the incentive for adversaries to target American forces stationed on their doorstep and eliminates the pressure to intervene in distant quarrels. True security lies not in policing the world, but in removing the targets that invite attack.

The existential threats of the 21st century – cyber warfare, climate change, pandemics, economic inequality, and potential great power conflict with near-peer adversaries like China or Russia – demand undivided attention and resources. Scattered across the globe, the US military is stretched thin, its forces and strategic focus fragmented. Bringing the troops home, consolidating defense capabilities, and focusing intelligence and diplomatic efforts solely on the defense of the continental United States allows for a more robust, agile, and technologically superior defense posture against the most pressing threats. It enables the concentration of national will and resources on building resilience at home.

Moreover, the US possesses powerful tools of influence short of direct military intervention: diplomacy, economic statecraft, targeted sanctions, humanitarian aid delivered through non-military channels, and the moral authority of its values. Security objections also arise, suggesting isolationism leaves America exposed. Disengagement removes the US from the role of global arbiter and nation-builder, acknowledging the limits of its power and the complex realities of other societies. It allows America to lead by example – through innovation, economic strength, scientific advancement, and the attractiveness of its democratic ideals – rather than through coercion and force. It fosters a foreign policy rooted in genuine national interest, avoiding the moral compromises inherent in propping up unpopular regimes or pursuing objectives detached from core American security and values.

The path of intervention has proven costly, counterproductive, and ultimately unsustainable. Isolationists argue the U.S. should be free to act purely in its own interest without external constraints or obligations.
    • Supposed Benefit: Unfettered Domestic Policy Autonomy: The U.S. government gains complete freedom to set its own policies on trade, environment, labor, and social issues without needing to comply with international standards or negotiate compromises with other nations. Important Caveats and Counterarguments:

It's crucial to note that this vision of isolationism is largely theoretical and faces significant practical and historical counterarguments:

  • Global Interdependence: The world economy is deeply interconnected. Disengaging could trigger economic recessions and harm key sectors.

The argument for complete U.S. isolationism posits that withdrawing from the world stage would fundamentally improve national well-being by eliminating the primary drivers of foreign wars, conserving immense resources for domestic priorities, removing motivations for foreign attacks, preserving absolute sovereignty, and fostering national unity. The core benefit is a nation focused entirely inward, free from external entanglements and threats, able to solve its own problems and prosper in isolation. While compelling in its simplicity and focus on domestic priorities, this vision faces profound practical challenges in an interconnected world where challenges rarely respect borders.

A local dispute involving an ally may escalate into a broader confrontation because treaty commitments compel intervention. A policy of total United States isolationism—complete withdrawal from all international alliances, closure of all overseas military bases, and full disengagement from foreign political and military involvement—is not a retreat born of fear or naïveté. Properly understood, it is a deliberate act of strategic self-respect, constitutional fidelity, and moral clarity. After nearly a century of expansive global entanglement, the United States has reached a point where continued interventionism is not only unsustainable, but corrosive to its security, prosperity, liberty, and democratic integrity. A decisive turn inward is not only justified; it is necessary.

  1. Restoring constitutional government and democratic accountability

Perpetual global engagement has normalized actions that would have horrified the framers of the Constitution.

  • War without genuine consent: Congress’s sole authority to declare war has been eroded by executive adventurism, “police actions,” undeclared interventions, covert operations, and open-ended Authorizations for Use of Military Force. Endless campaigns overseas proceed with little meaningful public debate, turning the gravest decision a republic can make—war—into a bureaucratic routine.

  • Democratic distortion: Foreign policy elites, defense contractors, and permanent security bureaucracies wield power wildly disproportionate to public consent. Alliances and “obligations” negotiated by small circles of officials effectively pre-commit the country to conflicts Americans never voted for and often oppose once the costs become clear.

Total isolationism—ending alliance commitments, dismantling foreign basing, and rejecting entangling security guarantees—re-aligns U.S. practice with its constitutional design: the people, through Congress, decide when, where, and whether the nation risks blood and treasure. Cutting off structural entanglements is the only reliable way to prevent drift into wars Americans did not explicitly choose.

  1. Ending the cycle of endless, counterproductive wars

The historical record of U.S. foreign intervention in the modern era is damning.

  • Military quagmires: Korea stalemated; Vietnam lost; Afghanistan collapsed after two decades; Iraq destabilized an entire region and helped incubate new terror threats; Libya fractured into chaos. Trillions spent, hundreds of thousands of lives lost or shattered, yet no lasting stability proportional to the cost.

  • Blowback: Interventions breed resentment, extremism, and anti-American militancy. Occupations, drone strikes, and proxy wars radicalize local populations and create the very threats they are ostensibly meant to prevent.

  • Constant mission creep: Humanitarian justifications morph into regime change; defensive efforts become nation-building; narrow objectives metastasize into decades-long commitments.

Total isolationism is the cleanest way to break this pattern. Partial restraint invariably gives way to “exceptions” and “limited strikes” that reopen the same destructive pathways. A categorical rule—no overseas bases, no alliances, no interventions—removes the structural incentives and opportunities that keep dragging the United States back into other peoples’ wars.

  1. Securing the homeland through defense, not dominion

Critics of isolationism insist that alliances and overseas deployments are bulwarks of U.S. security. In practice, they function as liabilities and provocations.

  • Tripwires for war: NATO guarantees, defense pacts, and security assurances transform regional disputes into potential U.S. obligations. A border clash in Eastern Europe, a naval skirmish in the South China Sea, or a crisis in the Middle East becomes a test of American “credibility,” risking escalation toward major power war.

  • Strategic overextension: Maintaining hundreds of bases and global commitments disperses resources, distracts leadership, and forces the U.S. to prepare for every contingency everywhere. This is the textbook definition of imperial overstretch.

  • Provoking arms races: U.S. forces parked on others’ borders inevitably inflame rival powers and fuel military buildups. The United States claims to preserve stability but often amplifies insecurity.

A total isolationist posture would mean:

  • No automatic defense of other nations.
  • No tripwire deployments.
  • A military configured purely for homeland defense: secure borders, robust air and naval defense, cyber protection, and a second-strike deterrent sufficient to make any attack suicidal.

Freed from imperial commitments, the United States could possess overwhelming defensive capability at a fraction of current cost, while drastically reducing the scenarios in which it is a target in the first place.

  • George Washington’s Farewell Address (1796): Warned against "permanent alliances" that could draw the U.S. into European conflicts.

In the rapidly shifting landscape of global politics, the United States has long maintained its position as a global superpower, underpinned by extensive military alliances, overseas bases, and active involvement in international conflicts. 1. Enhanced National Security and Autonomy

The primary rationale for isolationism lies in the protection of national sovereignty and security. By abandoning entanglements with foreign powers—whether through alliances or permanent military presence abroad—America eliminates the vulnerabilities inherent in collective defense arrangements. History is replete with examples of alliances being exploited: NATO’s involvement in the 2003 Iraq War, the U.S.'s obligations under the NATO Article 5, or the legacy of American troops stationed in Europe and the Middle East. Each of these commitments has exposed the U.S. to risks of betrayal, misalignment of interests, and unexpected entanglements in foreign crises. Complete isolation would remove these risks, allowing the U.S. to focus solely on its own defense needs and respond to threats based on its own strategic calculus, rather than those of allies with divergent priorities.

2. Economic Efficiency and Resource Optimization

Foreign military engagements are not only costly in terms of human lives and treasure but also drain national resources. The annual expenditures on overseas bases, combined with the costs of maintaining global troop deployments and supporting allied militaries, run into tens of billions of dollars. By closing all overseas bases and ending international commitments, the U.S. could reallocate these funds to domestic priorities: infrastructure, healthcare, education, and technological innovation. Moreover, isolationism would eliminate the economic risks associated with foreign entanglements, such as unexpected reparations, trade disputes, or the economic fallout from political misadventures abroad. America could focus its economic might entirely on its own citizens, fostering self-reliance and robust domestic growth.

3. Moral and Ethical Consistency

The United States has long professed to be a beacon of liberty and democracy. Yet, its foreign interventions—ranging from the Truman Doctrine to the War on Terror—have at times conflicted with these ideals, leading to controversial outcomes in countries such as Iraq, Afghanistan, and Syria. Critics argue that these actions have destabilized regions, fostered resentment, and undermined local governance. By embracing isolationism, the U.S. would align its foreign policy with its founding principles: non-interference in the internal affairs of other nations and a commitment to self-determination. This consistency could serve as a moral example to the world and reinforce America’s status as a principled, if not interventionist, global actor.

4. Reducing Global Instability—From the American Perspective

Paradoxically, some proponents of isolationism argue that by stepping back, the U.S. could avoid exacerbating the very global crises it seeks to address. Military interventions often lead to protracted conflicts, humanitarian disasters, and the rise of new powers at America’s expense. By staying on the sidelines, the U.S. might prevent itself from becoming a target of global antagonisms, or becoming embroiled in proxy wars that drag it into larger regional or even world conflicts. Furthermore, isolationism could allow the U.S. to act as a mediator or mediator-of-last-resort when absolutely necessary, rather than as a constant actor in others’ quarrels.

5. Reimagining American Power in a Multipolar World

The world is no longer unipolar; China, India, and other rising powers are reshaping global dynamics. By turning inward, the U.S. would recalibrate its role from that of a hegemon dictating terms to a formidable, if contained, power focused on its own development. This could foster respect from other nations, reduce the risk of overextension, and allow America to negotiate from a position of strength rather than dominance. In a world where power is distributed more evenly, isolationism may be a sustainable and less destabilizing approach.

Conclusion

Total U.S. isolationism is not a policy that appeals to the American love of freedom and global leadership in the traditional sense. Yet, for nations facing existential risks, escalating costs, and shifting global realities, it presents a calculated alternative. The sacrifices in global influence and soft power are real, but so are the potential gains in security, autonomy, and national well-being. In an era where the costs of engagement outweigh the benefits, the American people may find a path to strength not in perpetual outward reach, but in purposeful self-restraint—a return to the idea that true greatness lies in protecting one’s own soil, before projecting power abroad.

In a stunning display of cosmic irony, a coalition of screaming virtue-signalers, jazz-hand diplomats, and people who think “global citizen” is a LinkedIn badge—not a cry for help—have taken to the streets waving signs that read, “AMERICA CAN’T JUST LEAVE!”

No, you can’t. You’ve got a Netflix subscription.

Let us pause, dear reader, and consider the sacred logic of these so-called “internationalists.” They claim that if we withdraw from the world, “chaos will reign!” “Dictators will rise!” “The world will forget that we once had a decent IKEA furniture delivery system!”

But let me ask you this: Why, pray tell, do the same people who are begging us to “stay engaged” also refuse to hold the door for the guy behind them at CVS while muttering, “I don’t even know who you are, but you cost me 17 seconds of my life”?

There is a∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗√∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗ hypocrisy so dense, even NASA sent a probe to study it. They want us to save the planet from climate collapse… while ordering avocado toast in three different compostable bamboo containers that each require a separate drone to deliver.

Let’s break down their most “urgent” arguments — with the subtlety of a Trump tweet:

—

Argument #1: “If we pull out, China and Russia will dominate!”

Ah yes. Because nothing says “American global leadership” like us spending $2.3 trillion a year on military toys we’ve never even used… while the average American can’t afford an aspirin with insurance.

China dominates? Maybe. But do we really want to be their wingman? They have the Great Wall. We have a 1,900-mile border wall that’s mostly Instagram backdrops and bureaucratic C+ work. Their innovation? AI, 5G, drones. Ours? A TikTok dance challenge about “how to fold a fitted sheet without crying.”

If we’re worried about global dominance, let’s just admit it: We’ve already lost. Our national anthem is now a commercial jingle played over a Zoom funeral.

—

Argument #2: “We have moral obligations to help other nations!”

Really? Then why did your FEMA volunteer squad abandon Katrina victims to become a “personal brand” on YouTube? And why did your church donate $20,000 to “help refugees in Chad”… but refused to let your neighbor’s dog sleep in the garage?

Isolation isn’t cruel. It’s self-care with a passport.

Do you know what happens when you stop trying to fix the world? Things… slow down. Quietly. Peacefully. No one dies in an airstrike… because no one cares enough to launch one. People start making their own damn sandwiches. It’s called “the 1890s.” We should move in.

—

Argument #3: “But what about international trade? We need global supply chains!”

Oh no. The iPhones will stop.

Exactly.

Who needs five-step Touch ID authentication when you can just yell “Siri, buy me another phone” while holding up a book titled: How I Solved My Addiction to Surveillance Capitalism in 8 Days?

Get a manual typewriter. Eat local. Charge your phone with a hamster wheel. The only thing the world needs from us is our unemployment benefits, which we can mail to our former allies as a final “I’m sorry” gesture — wrapped in a FedEx envelope printed with the phrase: “I’m out. Actually, I’m not even mad.”

—

Argument #4: “But Ambassador Fritz has a daughter in Rwanda!”

Shouldn't she be allowed to choose her own destiny? Maybe she wants to live without American military drones buzzing overhead like angry hornets who think they’re peacekeepers.

If her daughter’s life depends on U.S. intervention, then maybe the problem isn’t the U.S. leaving — it’s that Rwanda was never supposed to have a smartphone.

Let her build her own WiFi. OWN her reconstruction. Become the Mali version of Elon Musk. With less robotics. More mutterings.

—

Final Thought: We’re Not Abandoning the World. We’re Evicting It.

For too long, we’ve been the world’s Uber driver — holding the door open while they spill their soy latte, talk about their therapist, and then leave us a 1-star review because the car smelled like “intersectional guilt.”

Here in America, we’ve mastered the art of pointing at other people’s problems while sucking on a member’s-only grape Pop-Tart.

So let us leave. Withdraw completely. Sell the UN building to a Kanye West fan club. Use the proceeds to fund a national nap time. Keep the aircraft carriers. Turn them into floating luxury casinos. That’s right. Vegas on the Pacific. Attendance: four people. All named Larry. Winners get an envelope with a single U.S. dollar and a sticky note:

> “You’re on your own now, buddy. We made it 300 years. We’re out.”

The world will survive. It already has — without our “help.” It just didn’t realize it until we stopped showing up with flapjacks and feel-good PowerPoint presentations titled: “Why America Must Stay.”

We didn’t leave. We just stopped auditioning for the role of the world’s emotional support nation.

And honestly? The world seems… calmer.

It’s like removing a loud dog that barks at squirrels for 12 hours a day. The neighborhood doesn’t crumble. It just… breathes.

So to all you “globalists” who think you can save the planet by posting a meme on LinkedIn: Go ahead. Take a picture of your reusable tote bag. Buy a $700 hemp yoga mat. And for sweet mercy — stay off my mail, my border, and my weirdly undisturbed silence.

We’re retiring. To the U.S.A.

It’s a great place. We finally have room to breathe.

… and no one to blame.

—
